rows.verified: Ladders are permitted where a risk assessment shows they are a sensible option for low-risk, short-duration work.
As a guide, alternative equipment should be considered if a task requires more than about 30 minutes at a time on a ladder or stepladder.
Ladder users must be competent or work under competent supervision, with training appropriate to the task.
The user should perform a pre-use visual check at the start of each working day and after changes such as dropping or moving the ladder.
Ladders should be used on firm, level, clean surfaces and protected from vehicles, doors, windows and public access.
A leaning ladder should be tied where possible; a stability device or secure wedging can be used where necessary, while footing is a last resort.
A ladder used for access should normally be tied and extend at least one metre above the landing point to provide a secure handhold.
Users should avoid overreaching, carry only light items, engage stepladder locks and maintain three points of contact at the working position.
Ladder suitability depends on task duration, height, surface, stability, securing method, public or vehicle interaction, load and user competence.
Ladder evidence is equipment-, task- and location-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fall probability.
Work near overhead electric lines must be carefully planned and carried out to avoid danger from contact or close proximity, even when the work is brief.
A person or object can be killed by flashover without physically touching a live overhead conductor.
High vehicles and long equipment such as cranes, MEWPs, tipper bodies, ladders, irrigation pipes and scaffold poles create particular risk.
Before work, overhead lines within or beside the work area and across access routes should be identified and assumed live unless their owner proves otherwise.
The line owner or distribution network operator should be consulted early so diversion, isolation or other precautions can be planned.
Danger should first be eliminated by avoiding the lines, diverting them or arranging for them to be made dead.
Where live-line danger cannot be eliminated, access and work should be controlled using barriers, defined passageways, goalposts and warning notices.
A line may re-energise automatically after tripping; equipment must not be disentangled until the line owner confirms it has been de-energised and made safe.
Overhead-line controls depend on voltage, line position, clearance, plant dimensions, access routes, ground conditions, weather and network-owner instructions.
Overhead-line evidence is line-, activity- and site-specific and is not an exact parcel-level electric-shock or flashover probability.
